title: Ἀλώπηξ καὶ δρυτόμος
part: The Fox and the Woodcutter (Chambry 34 · Perry 22)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 34 (= Perry 22). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ κυνηγοὺς φεύγουσα, ὡς ἐθεάσατό τινα δρυτόμον, τοῦτον ἱκέτευσε κατακρύψαι αὐτήν.
sentences.tr: Alōpēx kynēgous pheugousa, hōs etheasato tina drytomon, touton hiketeuse katakrypsai autēn.
sentences.l: A fox fleeing hunters, when she beheld a certain woodcutter, begged him to hide her.
sentences.n: φεύγω with a plain accusative is 'flee from'. ἱκετεύω, 'to come as a suppliant', is a strong word: it takes the accusative of the person implored and an infinitive of the thing asked, and it puts the fox formally under the man's protection. δρυτόμος is 'oak-cutter' (δρῦς + τέμνω), the ordinary word for a woodcutter.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ αὐτῇ παρῄνεσεν εἰς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ καλύβην εἰσελθοῦσαν κρυβῆναι.
sentences.tr: Ho de autēi parēinesen eis tēn heautou kalybēn eiselthousan krybēnai.
sentences.l: And he advised her, having gone into his own hut, to hide.
sentences.i: He told her to go into his hut and hide there.
sentences.n: παραινέω takes the dative of the person advised and an infinitive of the advice. εἰσελθοῦσαν is accusative because it agrees with the unexpressed subject of κρυβῆναι: Greek strings a participle onto an infinitive where English joins two verbs with 'and'. A καλύβη is a rough hut or cabin.

sentences.t: Μετ’ οὐ πολὺ δὲ παραγενομένων τῶν κυνηγῶν καὶ τοῦ δρυτόμου πυνθανομένων εἰ τεθέαται ἀλώπεκα τῇδε παριοῦσαν, ἐκεῖνος τῇ μὲν φωνῇ ἠρνεῖτο ἑωρακέναι, τῇ δὲ χειρὶ νεύων ἐσήμαινεν ὅπου κατεκρύπτετο.
sentences.tr: Met’ ou poly de paragenomenōn tōn kynēgōn kai tou drytomou pynthanomenōn ei tetheatai alōpeka tēide pariousan, ekeinos tēi men phōnēi ērneito heōrakenai, tēi de cheiri neuōn esēmainen hopou katekrypteto.
sentences.l: And not long after, the hunters having arrived and asking the woodcutter whether he had seen a fox passing by that way, he with his voice kept denying having seen her, but with his hand, making signs, kept indicating where she was hidden.
sentences.i: Not long after, the hunters came up and asked the woodcutter whether he had seen a fox go past that way; with his voice he denied having seen her, while with his hand he gestured towards where she was hiding.
sentences.n: Another genitive absolute (παραγενομένων … πυνθανομένων). τοῦ δρυτόμου is a genitive of a different kind standing beside it: πυνθάνομαι regularly takes the genitive of the person asked. εἰ introduces the indirect question, 'whether'; τεθέαται is a perfect kept as a perfect in indirect speech, where English shifts to 'had seen'. The μέν … δέ pair — τῇ μὲν φωνῇ against τῇ δὲ χειρί — is the whole fable in one line: the voice says one thing, the hand another.

sentences.t: Τῶν δὲ οὐχ οἷς ἔνευε προσσχόντων, οἷς δὲ ἔλεγε πιστευσάντων, ἡ ἀλώπηξ ἰδοῦσα αὐτοὺς ἀπαλλαγέντας ἐξελθοῦσα ἀπροσφωνητὶ ἐπορεύετο.
sentences.tr: Tōn de ouch hois eneue prosschontōn, hois de elege pisteusantōn, hē alōpēx idousa autous apallagentas exelthousa aprosphōnēti eporeueto.
sentences.l: But they not having attended to the things at which he was making signs, but having trusted the things he was saying, the fox, having seen them gone off, having come out, went on her way without a word.
sentences.i: They paid no heed to what he pointed at, but believed what he said; and the fox, seeing them gone, came out and went off without a word.
sentences.n: προσέχω, with τὸν νοῦν understood, means 'apply the mind to' and takes the dative — hence οἷς ἔνευε, 'the things at which he was making signs'. νεύω is to nod or beckon; the signing here is done with the hand, not the head. The two relative clauses have no antecedents at all, which is why English has to supply 'what'. ἀπροσφωνητί is a rare adverb, 'without a word of address' — she leaves without speaking, and that silence is what the woodcutter is about to complain of.

sentences.t: Μεμφομένου δὲ αὐτὴν τοῦ δρυτόμου, εἴγε διασωθεῖσα ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ διὰ φωνῆς αὐτῷ ἐμαρτύρησεν, ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ ἔγωγε ηὐχαρίστησα ἄν σοι, εἰ τοῖς λόγοις ὅμοια τὰ ἔργα τῆς χειρὸς καὶ τοὺς τρόπους εἶχες. »
sentences.tr: Memphomenou de autēn tou drytomou, eige diasōtheisa hyp’ autou, all’ oude dia phōnēs autōi emartyrēsen, ephē· « All’ egōge ēucharistēsa an soi, ei tois logois homoia ta erga tēs cheiros kai tous tropous eiches. »
sentences.l: And the woodcutter blaming her — that though she had been brought safely through by him, she had not even by voice borne witness for him — she said: « Well, I for my part would have thanked you, if you had had the works of your hand, and your ways, like your words. »
sentences.i: The woodcutter reproached her: though she had been saved by him, she had not so much as spoken a word for him. And she said, « I would have thanked you, if the work of your hand and your manners had matched your words. »
sentences.n: The reproach is loosely put even in Greek: a genitive absolute (Μεμφομένου … τοῦ δρυτόμου) followed by εἴγε, 'seeing that', and then ἀλλά resuming — 'granted she was saved by him, yet she did not…'. The syntax slips halfway into the man's own grumbling. The fox answers with an unreal condition: ἄν with the aorist indicative in the main clause and εἰ with the imperfect in the if-clause — 'I would have thanked you, if you had had…', with the plain implication that he did not. μαρτυρέω with the dative is to bear witness for someone, to speak up on his side.

sentences.t: Τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ χρήσαιτο ἄν τις πρὸς ἐκείνους τοὺς ἀνθρώπους τοὺς χρηστὰ μὲν σαφῶς ἐπαγγελλομένους, δι’ ἔργων δὲ φαῦλα δρῶντας.
sentences.tr: Toutōi tōi logōi chrēsaito an tis pros ekeinous tous anthrōpous tous chrēsta men saphōs epangellomenous, di’ ergōn de phaula drōntas.
sentences.l: This story someone might use against those men who plainly promise good things, but through their deeds do base ones.
sentences.i: One might use this story against people who plainly promise fair things but in their actions do shabby ones.
sentences.n: The moral opens with a potential optative, χρήσαιτο ἄν τις — 'one might use' — the same formula as the astronomer's fable (65); χράομαι takes the dative of the thing used. μέν … δέ again holds words apart from deeds, exactly as the woodcutter's voice was held apart from his hand.
